title: Data Modeling & Database Design
concepts: Master-detail: the child has no owner of its own and inherits sharing from the parent. Deleting the parent deletes the children. Roll-up summary fields work natively.
Lookup: a loose link. The child keeps its own owner and sharing, and the field can be optional.
Hierarchical relationships exist only on the User object (for example, Manager).
External lookup links a standard or custom child to an external object by External ID. Indirect lookup links an external child to a Salesforce parent through a unique External ID field on the parent.
Big Objects store billions of records with consistent performance. You query them through their defined index, so design the index first.
Person Accounts merge Account and Contact for B2C. Once enabled, they can't be turned off.
Contacts to Multiple Accounts uses the AccountContactRelation junction. Each contact still has one primary account.
Junction objects (two master-detail fields) model many-to-many relationships.
rules: Need roll-ups and cascade delete with tight ownership? Master-detail.
High-volume child inserts against a few parents? Prefer lookup, because master-detail locks the parent on every child insert or update.
Data that only needs to be viewed, not reported on or automated in Salesforce? Virtualize it with Salesforce Connect and external objects.
Long-term archive inside the platform, read mostly? Big Object.
A picklist is cheaper than a lookup when many records would point at a few values (avoids lookup skew).
numbers: Keep each parent under 10,000 child records (account data skew).
Keep each user under 10,000 owned records (ownership skew).
traps: Changing master-detail to lookup is allowed only when no roll-up summary fields exist on the parent.
Reports, triggers and flows on Big Objects are limited. Don't propose them for day-to-day transactional data.
keywords: "millions of child records under one account" means data skew, so redesign the hierarchy
"only needs to display data from ERP" means Salesforce Connect, not an import

title: Master Data Management
concepts: The golden record is the single trusted version of an entity (customer, product) built from several sources.
Survivorship rules decide which source wins for each field (most recent, most trusted system, most complete).
Registry style: the hub keeps only a cross-reference of IDs. Data stays in the source systems.
Consolidation style: the hub builds a golden record for reporting. Sources are not updated.
Coexistence style: the hub builds the golden record and syncs it back to the sources.
Centralized (transaction) style: the hub is where master data is created and edited. Sources subscribe.
rules: Salesforce can be the system of record or a system of engagement. Decide per entity, then define which system owns each field.
Use External IDs to keep cross-references between Salesforce and other systems.
traps: Duplicate Management de-duplicates inside one org. It is not an MDM hub.
keywords: "single view of the customer across ERP and CRM" means MDM plus golden record
"source systems must stay untouched" means Registry or Consolidation

title: Large Data Volume Considerations
verified: Numbers in this chapter were checked against the LDV whitepaper (Summer '25).
concepts: The query optimizer runs a pre-query against index statistics to decide whether an index is selective enough to use.
Skinny tables hold frequently used fields from one object to avoid joins. Only Salesforce Support can create or change them, and they stay in sync automatically.
Indexed by default: record Id, Name, lookup and master-detail fields (including OwnerId), RecordTypeId, Division, CreatedDate, SystemModstamp, and Email on Contact and Lead.
External ID fields (Auto Number, Email, Number, Text) are indexed automatically.
Custom indexes exclude null values unless Support enables null indexing.
Divisions partition very large orgs (needs over 1 million records in an object and more than 35 licenses).
Defer sharing calculation suspends sharing recalculation during big loads or realignments.
Soft-deleted records sit in the Recycle Bin for 15 days and still affect performance. Use Bulk API hard delete for very large deletes.
PK chunking splits a big Bulk API query into ranges of record IDs.
rules: Make filters selective: index the field and keep the filter under the threshold.
AND filters use indexes unless one returns more than 20% of records or 666,666 records.
OR filters need every field indexed, and each under 10% or 333,333 records.
Deleting 1 million or more records: use the hard delete option of Bulk API or Bulk API 2.0. Delete children first.
Use a data-tiering strategy: keep active data on core objects, archive the rest.
numbers: Standard index: used if the filter matches under 30% of the first 1M records and under 15% of the rest, max 1,000,000 records.
Custom index: used if the filter matches under 10% of total records, max 333,333 records.
Skinny tables: max 200 columns, no fields from other objects, copied only to Full sandboxes.
Skew limit: 10,000 children per parent and 10,000 records per owner.
traps: Negative filters (!=, NOT IN), leading-wildcard LIKE, and non-deterministic formulas are not selective.
A custom index on a field where most rows share one value does nothing.
Skinny tables are not a fix for everything. They add maintenance overhead.
keywords: "tens of millions of records and report timeouts" means selectivity, skinny tables or archiving
"UNABLE_TO_LOCK_ROW during load" means lock contention, so sort by parent or reduce parallelism

title: Salesforce Data Management
concepts: Matching rules define how records are compared (exact or fuzzy, field by field).
Duplicate rules define what happens when a match is found: allow with alert, report, or block.
Upsert with an External ID inserts or updates without needing the Salesforce record ID.
Data quality dimensions: completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, uniqueness, validity.
State and Country picklists standardize address data at entry.
Validation rules, required fields, picklists and lookup filters prevent bad data at the source.
rules: Prevent duplicates at entry with duplicate rules. Clean existing duplicates with reports, merge, or an AppExchange tool.
Integrations should upsert on an External ID instead of querying for Salesforce IDs first.
traps: A matching rule alone does nothing. It must be used by an active duplicate rule.
keywords: "stop users creating duplicate leads" means matching rule plus duplicate rule (block or alert)
"sync without storing Salesforce IDs in ERP" means External ID upsert

title: Data Migration
concepts: SOAP and REST APIs are synchronous and suited to small, real-time volumes.
Bulk API processes records asynchronously in batches. Bulk API 2.0 handles batching for you.
Parallel processing is fast but can cause lock contention when children share a parent. Bulk API 1.0 offers serial mode; Bulk API 2.0 does not let you choose.
Tasks can lock both the related What and Who records during loads.
Batch Apex processes very large record sets in chunks inside the platform.
rules: Load parents before children and link them through External IDs.
Sort child records by parent ID so one batch holds one parent's children.
Before a big load: disable or bypass triggers, flows and validation rules where safe, and consider deferring sharing calculation.
Extract huge tables with Bulk API query plus PK chunking.
traps: Serial mode fixes locking but is slow. Sorting by parent is usually the better first fix.
Gemini's claim about CSV header case causing silent nulls is unverified. Don't rely on it.
keywords: "millions of records, overnight load" means Bulk API
"lock errors on child inserts" means sort by parent ID or go serial

title: Data Governance
concepts: Governance roles: data owners, data stewards, and a governance council that sets standards.
Data classification fields on each field: Data Owner, Field Usage, Data Sensitivity Level, Compliance Categorization.
Field History Tracking records field changes for a limited period.
Shield Field Audit Trail keeps field history much longer, stored in a Big Object.
Backup and restore is the customer's responsibility. Plan full, incremental and partial backups and test restores.
rules: Regulated data with long retention needs: Field Audit Trail, not standard history.
Assign a steward per data domain and track quality metrics.
numbers: Field History Tracking: up to 20 fields per object. Data shown for 18 months, available via API for 24 months.
Field Audit Trail: up to 60 fields per object, retention up to 10 years.
traps: Field-level security controls visibility. It is not an audit trail.
keywords: "auditors need 7 years of field changes" means Shield Field Audit Trail
